title: Similitude 1: Two cities, two laws
sum: The Similitudes, the third part of the book, begin with the shortest parable. Christians live in a foreign city whose lord has his own laws; their own city is far away, with a law of its own. A citizen of heaven who piles up fields and houses here cannot go home, and when the lord of this city throws him out for keeping his own law, everything he built is lost (50:1-5). So keep only what is enough, and spend the rest on "fields" in the other city: souls in distress, widows and orphans (50:6-9). That is a lavish spending that is "good and holy" (50:10).

Lake's English calls these sections "Parables" (Greek parabolai); the Latin version's similitudines gave them their usual name, the Similitudes (Lake's note on the heading). The site names the division Similitude 1-10 and says "parable" in the text. Lake's heading above the division is "The parables which he spoke with me"; part of the Greek here, as for the rest of the book after 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6), rests on the Athos manuscript alone.

views.H: From here to 107:2 the continuous Greek is the Athos manuscript (A), copied by Simonides and "very inaccurate" (Lake), checked where papyri, the Latin and Ethiopic versions, and quotations survive. Lake's note on 50:2 shows the versions reading a different verb.
views.N: The two cities are Hebrews 13:14 (Lake's note: "For here have we no continuing city"), Philippians 3:20 and 1 Peter 2:11; the care of widows and orphans is James 1:27, in Lake's margin.
views.D: The parable is often cited on Christian use of property. It does not forbid ownership but limits it to "what is enough" (50:6) and turns surplus into almsgiving.
views.R: Rome was full of foreigners living under a law not their own, and of freedmen and slaves who could lose everything at a master's word. Hermas, once sold as a slave (1:1), uses the figure of a resident who can be expelled at the city lord's will.

echoes: Hebrews 13:14; Hebrews 11:13-16; Philippians 3:20; 1 Peter 2:11; James 1:27; Matthew 6:19-21; Luke 12:16-21; Epistle to Diognetus 5:5

settings.what: The parable of the two cities
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas; through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1; 77:1)
settings.when: the first of the parables, after the twelve Mandates (26-49)
settings.why: To loosen believers' hold on property: whoever builds a life in this city cannot go home to the city of God, and wealth is meant for the poor.
settings.readers: Christians in Rome, Hermas's city (1:1), among whom were people with fields, houses and "costly estates"; Hermas himself had been in business (3:1).

title: Similitude 2: The elm and the vine
sum: Walking in the country, Hermas looks at a vine growing up an elm. The Shepherd explains: the elm bears no fruit and the vine on the ground bears little, but together they give a full crop (51:3-4). So with the rich and the poor in the church. The rich man is poor toward God, distracted by his wealth, and his prayer is weak; the poor man is rich in prayer. When the rich supplies the poor man's needs, the poor man prays for him, and both "complete the work" (51:5-7). In a drought the elm's water keeps the vine alive (51:8). Both are "partners in the righteous work" (51:9).

The parable gives the rich a place in the church without flattering them. It assumes that the poor man's prayer has real power with God and that the rich man's wealth is given "from the Lord" for this service.

views.H: Two papyri cover this chapter: Oxyrhynchus 1172 (Similitude 2.4-10, 51:4-10) and Berlin 5513 (Similitude 2.7-10, 51:7-10), by Lake's introduction. Lake's text of 51:5 and 51:8 depends on a reading from the papyrus and on a modern conjecture (see the variants).
views.N: The rich who are poor toward God (Luke 12:21) and the poor who are rich in faith (James 2:5); the exchange of gifts between churches in 2 Corinthians 8:13-15, where each one's surplus supplies the other's lack.
views.J: That God hears the poor is a theme of the Psalms (Psalm 34:6) and of Jewish teaching on charity, which Hermas carries into the church.
views.D: The parable treats the prayers of the poor as a real help to those who give to them (51:5-6), but it speaks of partnership and gratitude, not of payment.
views.R: Vines trained on trees were a common sight in Italy. The relation of a rich patron and a poor client, who owed his patron loyalty and greetings, was a basic Roman social bond; Hermas recasts it as a partnership before God.

echoes: Luke 12:21; James 2:5; 2 Corinthians 8:13-15; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; Psalm 34:6; Galatians 2:10

settings.what: The parable of the elm and the vine
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, walking in the field (51:1); through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1; 77:1)
settings.when: as Hermas walks in a field
settings.why: To bind the rich and poor of the church together: the rich give, the poor pray, and each fills up what the other lacks.
settings.readers: A Roman congregation with both rich and poor members; the Visions blame Hermas's own household for being corrupted by business (3:1), so the warning came from inside such a church.

title: Similitude 3: Trees in winter
sum: The Shepherd shows Hermas many leafless trees that all look dry. In this world, he says, the righteous and sinners look alike, as trees do in winter, when no one can tell the dead from the living (52:1-3). The short parable sets up the next one, which shows the same trees in summer.

views.N: The weeds and the wheat that grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30) and Paul's "stop judging before the right time, until the Lord comes" (1 Corinthians 4:5).
views.J: "This world" (Greek "this age") and "the age that is coming" (52:2; 53:2) are the two ages of Jewish hope, used throughout the New Testament (Matthew 12:32).
views.D: The parable is a caution against trying to sort the church into the pure and the impure now. That fits Hermas's message of repentance: no one is to be written off before the summer.

settings.what: The parable of the trees in winter
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas; through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1; 77:1)
settings.when: after the elm and the vine
settings.why: To explain why righteous and sinful believers cannot yet be told apart, and to warn against judging by appearances.
settings.readers: Roman Christians who, in a church with both faithful and lapsed members (as Similitude 8 describes), might be tempted to sort one another.

title: Similitude 4: Trees in summer
sum: Now some trees are budding and some are dry. The age that is coming is summer for the righteous and winter for sinners: when the Lord's mercy shines out, each tree's fruit will show (53:1-3). The nations and the sinners will be found dry and will be burned like wood, sinners because they did not repent, the nations because they did not know their Creator (53:4).

The Shepherd ends with practical advice for a man of business: bear fruit, and stay out of too many dealings. Those who do many things sin in many things and do not serve the Lord; those who serve him receive what they ask. One business, done with a pure mind, leaves room to serve God (53:5-8).

views.H: Lake's introduction lists Berlin papyrus 5513 as holding Similitude 4.2-5 (53:2-5), and the Hamburg fragment as holding Similitude 4.6-7 (53:6-7). Lake's notes record only one small difference here (53:5, μηδέν A, μηδέ L).
views.N: The fruit that shows the tree (Matthew 7:16-20; 12:33), the burning of fruitless trees (Matthew 3:10; John 15:6), and the soldier who does not get tangled in business (2 Timothy 2:4).
views.J: The nations judged for not knowing their Creator is the argument of Wisdom of Solomon 13 and Romans 1:20-21.
views.R: Rome was a city of trade. Hermas speaks to merchants and businessmen in the church: he limits business rather than forbidding it.

echoes: Matthew 7:16-20; Matthew 3:10; John 15:6; Romans 1:20-21; 2 Timothy 2:4; Malachi 4:1-2

settings.what: The parable of the trees in summer
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas; through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1; 77:1)
settings.when: right after the trees in winter
settings.why: To give hope to the righteous, warn sinners that the age that is coming will show their fruit, and tell busy believers to limit their business.
settings.readers: Merchants and property owners in the Roman church, whom the book warns again in 74:1-2 and 75:1.

title: Similitude 5.1: The fast that God accepts
sum: Similitude 5 begins with a fast. Hermas is sitting on a mountain at dawn, fasting and giving thanks, when the Shepherd sits down beside him. "I am keeping a station," Hermas says: a fast day (54:1-2). The Shepherd answers that this fast is useless. God does not want an empty fast; the fast he accepts is a life of obedience: no evil, a pure heart, the commandments kept, no evil desire, faith in God (54:3-5).
The word "station" (statiōn) comes from Latin army language. Lake notes that it "is not found elsewhere in Greek writers," while Latin writers use it "in the sense of a fixed time for fasting."

views.H: The Hamburg fragment (H), which begins at 53:6, continues here; Lake's note at 54:3 gives a line found only in H and one Latin version (see the variant).
views.N: The teaching follows Jesus on fasting (Matthew 6:16-18) and the commandments (Matthew 19:17, in Lake's margin), and Isaiah 58, which Barnabas 3 quotes for the same point.
views.J: Isaiah 58 and Zechariah 7-8 are the prophets' critique of fasts without justice; Jewish fasting on fixed days (the Didache 8:1 mentions Monday and Thursday for "the hypocrites") was the background to Christian fast days.
views.D: The site's cards on fixed fast days are at Judith 8 and Matthew 4 and 6. Hermas does not abolish the station but redefines it.
views.R: Statio was a soldier's post. Lake quotes Tertullian, who says (in the site's translation of his Latin) that the station "takes its name from the army, for we too are God's soldiers."

echoes: Isaiah 58:3-7; Zechariah 7:5-10; Matthew 6:16-18; Matthew 19:17; Joel 2:12-13; Epistle of Barnabas 3:1-5; Didache 8:1

settings.what: The Shepherd's teaching on the true fast
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, fasting at dawn on a mountain (54:1); through him the Roman church
settings.when: while Hermas keeps a "station" (a fast day)
settings.why: To teach that fasting without obedience is empty, and that the real fast is a life kept from evil.
settings.readers: Roman Christians, to whom Hermas speaks of a fast day as a "station," a word Lake finds in no other Greek writer, though Latin writers such as Tertullian use it for a fixed time of fasting.

deep.b: Hermas's answer "I have a station" (statiōna echō) needs explaining even to the angel ("What is a station?"). Lake's English note: "'Station' is not found elsewhere in Greek writers but is used in Latin writers in the sense of a fixed time for fasting (e.g. cf. Tertullian de orat. 19, de jejun. 1, 10, etc.). It is apparently one of the many terms taken from military language." The site's other fasting passages (Didache 8:1 on fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays; Matthew 6:16-18) show that fixed fast days were early. Hermas's own fast is to end with bread and water and a gift to the poor (56:7).

title: Similitude 5.2: The parable of the slave in the vineyard
sum: The Shepherd tells a parable "that has to do with fasting." A man plants a vineyard and gives it to a faithful slave with one order: put stakes in it, and you will be free. The slave stakes it, then on his own digs and weeds it too, and it thrives (55:2-4). The master returns, is delighted, calls his beloved son and his friends, and decides to make the slave an heir together with his son (55:5-8). Later the master sends dishes from a dinner, and the slave keeps what he needs and shares the rest with his fellow slaves, who pray for him; the master and his son agree all the more (55:9-11).

Every piece of the story comes from Jesus' parables: the vineyard, the journey abroad, the slave left in charge, the beloved son and heir. But the plot runs the other way: here the slave who does more than he is told is made a son. The angel will explain it three ways: about the fast (56), about the Son of God (58-59), and about the believer's flesh (59:5-60:4).

views.H: Lake suspects a gap in 55:2 (the master's departure); the Latin puts it first. The Athos manuscript is the only continuous Greek here, with the Hamburg fragment for part of Similitude 5.
views.N: Mark 12:1-9 and Matthew 21:33-41 (the vineyard, the beloved son, the heir); Luke 17:7-10 (the slave who does only what is ordered, here exceeded); Romans 8:17 and Galatians 4:7 (from slave to heir); John 15:15 (no longer slaves, but friends).
views.J: The vineyard is Israel's oldest picture of God's people (Isaiah 5:1-7; Psalm 80:8-16), which the explanation keeps: "the vines are this people" (58:2).
views.D: The parable's slave does good beyond the order and is rewarded with more glory (56:3): an early text in the long argument over works beyond what God commands. See the note on 56:3.
views.R: Roman masters freed trusted slaves, and a freedman could be well placed. Hermas, sold as a slave in his youth (1:1), gives the slave's freedom and adoption a central place.

echoes: Mark 12:1-9; Matthew 21:33-41; Luke 17:7-10; Matthew 25:14-30; Romans 8:17; Galatians 4:1-7; Isaiah 5:1-7

settings.what: The parable of the slave in the vineyard
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, on the mountain where he was fasting; through him the Roman church
settings.when: after the teaching on the true fast
settings.why: To show, through a story, the fast that pleases God (obedience plus good done freely) and, as the angel will explain, the work and reward of the Son of God.
settings.readers: A church with many slaves and freedmen, for whom freedom and adoption into a master's family were concrete hopes; Hermas himself had been sold as a slave (1:1).

title: Similitude 5.3: How to keep the fast
sum: Hermas asks for an explanation. The Shepherd first gives the lesson for the fast: whoever keeps the commandments and does some good beyond what God commands wins more glory (56:3). The fast is good when the commandments are kept (56:5). First guard against every evil word and desire and clean the heart (56:6). Then on the fast day eat only bread and water, add up what the day's food would have cost, and give it to a widow or orphan or someone in need, so that the one who receives may pray for you (56:7). Such a fast is a sacrifice God accepts, written down in heaven, for Hermas and his whole household (56:8-9).
It describes how to keep a fast, and it joins fasting to almsgiving, as Isaiah 58:7 did.

views.H: At 56:3 Lake prints the short Greek of A, though most editors take a longer sentence from the Latin; at 56:8 Lake's note shows Antiochus of Palestine and pseudo-Athanasius quoting this verse, the start of the book's ancient quotation trail.
views.N: Matthew 6:16-18 (fasting in secret), Philippians 4:18 and Hebrews 13:16 (gifts as sacrifices), Luke 17:10 (doing what is commanded).
views.J: Fasting joined to charity is the teaching of Isaiah 58:6-7: "to break your bread for the hungry" (Isaiah 58:7).
views.D: "If you do some good beyond what God commands" (56:3) has been read in arguments over works of supererogation; the churches' answers are set out on the card at Luke 17:10. Fixed fast days are asked about on the cards at Judith 8 and Matthew 6.
views.R: The widow and the orphan were the poorest people of a Roman city, without a male protector or income. Hermas's household was to keep the fast together (56:9).

echoes: Isaiah 58:6-7; Matthew 6:16-18; Luke 17:10; Philippians 4:18; Hebrews 13:16; James 1:27

settings.what: Rules for the fast
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas and, through him, his children and household (56:9) and all who hear
settings.when: Hermas has asked for the parable to be explained
settings.why: To give a practical rule: guard the heart, eat bread and water, and give the day's food money to the poor.
settings.readers: Roman Christian households that kept station days; the widows of the church, whom Grapte was to teach (8:3), are among those who would receive the gift.

title: Similitude 5.4: Hermas insists on the meaning
sum: Hermas begs the Shepherd to explain every part of the parable. The angel scolds him for asking: whoever has the Lord in his heart can ask God for understanding (57:2-4). Hermas answers that since the angel is with him he must ask him (57:5). The short chapter is a dialogue about how revelation works: by asking.

views.N: James 1:5-8 (ask God for wisdom without doubting); Mark 4:10-13 and 4:34 (the disciples ask, and Jesus explains privately).
views.J: The seer who questions his angel guide is a fixture of Jewish apocalypses (Daniel 7:16; 12:8; 4 Ezra 4-5).
views.D: Hermas has been "made strong by the holy angel" (57:4) and received prayer from him: angels here help a believer to pray. Whether this angel is Christ, Michael or another is not said.

echoes: James 1:5-8; Mark 4:10-13; Mark 4:34; Daniel 7:16; Daniel 12:8; 4 Ezra 4:22-25

settings.what: Hermas asks for the parable to be explained
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: after the rules for the fast
settings.why: To teach that understanding comes to those who ask God, while letting Hermas's questions draw out the explanation for the church.
settings.readers: The Roman church that would read the book, which is shown here how its revelations came: by Hermas's persistent asking.

title: Similitude 5.5: The parable explained
sum: Because Hermas keeps asking, the Shepherd explains the parable "so that you can make it known to everyone" (58:1). The field is this world; the lord of the field is God the Creator; the slave is the Son of God; the vines are this people; the stakes are the holy angels; the weeds are the lawless acts of God's slaves; the dishes are the commandments given through the Son; the friends are the first-created angels; the master's journey is the time left until his coming (58:2-3). Hermas then asks the question every reader asks: why is the Son of God a slave in the story? (58:5).

Lake notes that the explanation leaves the son of the parable unexplained: the slave is the Son of God, but who is the master's own beloved son and heir? That gap is one of the puzzles of Similitude 5.

views.H: One Latin version adds to 58:2, "but the Son is the Holy Spirit" (see the variant). Lake's English notes point out that the parable's son "remains unexplained" and that the master's absence is not in the parable's text as it stands (see 55:2).
views.N: The point-by-point method copies Jesus' explanation of the weeds (Matthew 13:37-43; "The field is the world," in Lake's margin). The question of 58:5 invites comparison with Philippians 2:6-11.
views.J: God taking counsel with angels (58:3; 59:4) recalls the heavenly council of 1 Kings 22:19-22 and Job 1-2, and angels as guardians of God's people (Daniel 10-12).
views.D: Calling the Son "the slave" was not a problem for Paul (Philippians 2:7); what is harder is that the explanation seems to separate the Son from the master's son and to make the slave's reward a promotion. The next chapter takes this up.

echoes: Matthew 13:37-43; Philippians 2:6-11; Isaiah 52:13; Mark 10:45; 1 Kings 22:19-22; Daniel 12:1

settings.what: The Shepherd explains the parable
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, on the mountain where he was fasting (54:1); through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1)
settings.when: after Hermas's persistent asking
settings.why: To give each part of the parable its meaning, so that Hermas can make it known to everyone.
settings.readers: The Roman church that heard the book, many of them slaves or former slaves, who would hear the Son of God described in a slave's role.

title: Similitude 5.6: The Son, the Spirit and the flesh
sum: The Shepherd answers: the Son of God is not in a slave's role but in "great authority and lordship" (59:1). God created the people and handed them to his Son; the Son put angels over them, cleansed their sins with much toil, showed them the paths of life and gave them the law he received from his Father (59:2-3). Then a second explanation: the Holy Spirit, who existed before and created all creation, God made to live in the flesh he wanted. That flesh served the Spirit well as a slave, kept it undefiled, and so God chose the flesh as the Spirit's partner and, with the Son and the angels as advisers, gave it a place and a reward (59:5-7). Every believer's flesh in which the Spirit lives will be rewarded if it stays pure (59:7).

This chapter is the center of the long debate over Hermas's Christology. Neither "Jesus" nor "Christ" appears in it, and the same parable seems to be read twice: once with the slave as the Son, once with the slave as the flesh in which the Spirit lived. The readings are set out below.

views.H: The Athos manuscript is the only continuous Greek. Lake's text supplies a "not" in 59:1 and a clause in 59:7 from the Latin and Ethiopic, and reports a Latin addition after 59:3; at 59:6 the Latin versions add an object to "pleased" ("God" or "the Lord"). See the variants.
views.N: The Son who "made a cleansing for sins" (Hebrews 1:3); the command the Son received from the Father (John 10:18; 12:49, in Lake's margin); the obedience that leads to exaltation (Philippians 2:8-9; Hebrews 5:8-9); but creation through the Spirit, not through the Son (contrast John 1:3; Colossians 1:16).
views.J: Jewish writings spoke of God's Spirit and Wisdom as present at creation (Genesis 1:2; Proverbs 8:22-31; Wisdom of Solomon 9:1-2, 17). Hermas's pre-existent Spirit who "created all creation" stands close to that Jewish language.
views.D: Later creeds distinguished the Son (the Word, through whom all things were made) from the Holy Spirit, and confessed one person of the Son with a full human nature. The question here is how to read an early writer who did not yet use those terms, not which church is right.
views.R: A slave who served well, was freed and adopted as heir, was a Roman story of reward. Hermas's Christology is told in that social language: service, partnership, inheritance.

echoes: John 1:1-3; John 1:14; Philippians 2:6-11; Hebrews 1:2-3; Hebrews 5:8-9; Romans 1:3-4; Acts 2:36; 1 Corinthians 6:19; 78:1; 89:2

settings.what: The Son's authority and the flesh in which the Spirit lived
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, on the mountain where he was fasting (54:1); through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (58:1)
settings.when: in answer to Hermas's question why the Son is a slave in the parable
settings.why: To show the Son's true authority, and to make the parable a pattern for every believer: the flesh that serves the Spirit purely will share its reward.
settings.readers: Roman Christians in a church where (by Lake's note on 60:2) some taught that the flesh does not matter; the chapter gives them a reason to keep the body pure. On the book's date, see the book's introduction.
views: The chapter is mainly about who the Son is (59:1-6), and the moral lesson (59:7; 60) follows. Harnack reads it this way, as the clearest witness to an adoptionist Christology (see below).
The chapter's aim is the believer's purity (59:7; 60:1-4), and its statements about the Son serve that lesson. Chapman: "As a layman, Hermas avoids dogma."

deep.b:
Adoptionist. Adolf von Harnack (History of Dogma, vol. 1) calls the Shepherd the one work "preserved entire which gives clear expression to the Adoptian Christology" (citing Similitude 5 and 9.1, 12): the Holy Spirit is "the pre-existent Son of God"; "the Redeemer is the virtuous man (sarx) chosen by God, with whom that Spirit of God was united," who, because he kept the Spirit undefiled and "did more than he was commanded," was "adopted as a son and exalted." Harnack adds that later adoptionists in Rome claimed their view had once been the Roman one (he cites Eusebius, Church History 5.28.3), and that this claim, "though exaggerated, is not incredible after what we find in Hermas."

A Spirit Christology, unclear rather than heretical. John Chapman (Catholic Encyclopedia, 1910) writes that "it has been thought with some reason that he did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Ghost" and that "he held that the Holy Ghost became the Son by His Incarnation," but that his ideas "may have been rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous"; "as a layman, Hermas avoids dogma." Lake's English note on 59:6 reads the passage the same way: the flesh, "in which the Spirit had been incarnate," became companion "of the Father and of the Son who is the Spirit."

Near to later orthodoxy. Philip Schaff (History of the Christian Church, vol. 2) says that in Hermas the Son "is represented as pre-existent and strictly divine," that Hermas "seems to identify his pre-existent divine nature with the Holy Spirit," and, in his note on the Spirit as the Son in Similitude 9.1 (78:1), that "a passage in a parable must not be pressed and it is differently explained," pointing to Hilgenfeld, Harnack, Zahn and Link for the explanations. He judges that the book's "meagre view of Christianity, far from being heretical or schismatic, is closely connected with catholic orthodoxy."

Angel Christology. Hermas also speaks of a "glorious angel" who in Similitude 9 is the Son of God and in Similitude 8 is called Michael (69:3). Lake's note there says that this, together with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit (he compares Similitude 5), "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas," and Harnack writes that "it is not certain whether he [the Spirit-Son] is identified with the chief Archangel." The text leaves open whether the Son is here pictured as the highest angel (see the chapter page of 69).

deep.title: Claude's theory: one parable, two hearings
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not a published view I have found stated this way. The explanation of Similitude 5 reads like two layers. In 59:2-3 the slave is the Son, and his toil is the cleansing of sins, a reading for the church about Christ. In 59:5-7 the slave is "the flesh" that served the indwelling Spirit and was made its partner, a reading that the very next sentence applies to "all flesh" (59:7) and then to Hermas's own body (60:1-4). Hermas may be using the Son's story as the pattern of every believer's story, so that the believer who keeps the Spirit undefiled becomes, like the slave, a fellow heir. If so, the chapter's puzzling Christology comes partly from making Christ the model of the penitent, which is the book's whole concern. Harnack noticed the parallel between Jesus and believers in Hermas (citing Similitude 5.6-7) but drew from it a different conclusion, that the view was adoptionist.

title: Similitude 5.7: Keep your flesh pure
sum: The Shepherd applies the parable to Hermas: keep this flesh of yours pure, so that the spirit living in it may testify for it (60:1). Never think the flesh is perishable and so free to misuse; defiling the flesh defiles the Holy Spirit (60:2). Hermas asks about sins done in ignorance before this teaching; the Shepherd answers that God alone can heal them, if from now on flesh and spirit are both kept pure, for they belong together (60:3-4).

views.H: At 60:2 every witness reads "if you defile the flesh," and Lake keeps it against editors who change it to "the spirit." At 60:3 the Latin, and A in part, add a promise of healing for former sins, which Lake says editors "(probably rightly)" accept.
views.N: 1 Corinthians 6:13-20 (the body for the Lord, a temple of the Holy Spirit); 2 Corinthians 7:1 (clean from every defilement of flesh and spirit); Acts 17:30 (times of ignorance).
views.D: Lake reads 60:2 as aimed at the "Gnostic tendency" to treat the body's acts as unimportant, and links it with the church's hope of the resurrection of the flesh. The healing of earlier sins "if from now on" the person stays pure is the book's teaching of one repentance in small.
views.R: Greek and Roman thought often set a perishable body against an immortal soul; Hermas insists that the two "belong together" (60:4).

settings.what: The lesson for Hermas's own flesh
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: after the explanation of the flesh in which the Spirit lived
settings.why: To make the parable personal: keep the body pure, because flesh and spirit are defiled together and saved together.
settings.readers: Roman Christians who, by Lake's reading, were meeting teachers who said that what the body does does not matter.

title: Similitude 6.1: The commandments and the young shepherd
sum: Similitude 6 opens with Hermas at home, praising God for the commandments and saying he will be blessed if he walks in them. The Shepherd appears and tells him not to be double-minded about them: they are good for those who are going to repent, and without them repentance is empty (61:1-4). Then he takes Hermas to a plain and shows him a young shepherd in saffron-yellow clothes, grazing a large flock of sheep that skip and frolic, living in luxury (61:5-6).

views.N: Putting on and taking off virtues and vices like clothes (Romans 13:12-14; Colossians 3:9-12); repentance shown in deeds (Acts 26:20).
views.J: The image of God's people as sheep and their leaders as shepherds is Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 11; here the shepherds are angels.
views.D: "These commandments are good for those who are going to repent" (61:3) states the book's structure: the Mandates are the rule of life for penitents.
views.R: Flocks grazing in the countryside around Rome were part of Hermas's world; the saffron-colored suit marks the young shepherd as showy and festive.

settings.what: The Shepherd's charge about the commandments
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, at home
settings.when: as Hermas praises God for the commandments
settings.why: To end the Mandates' teaching with a warning against double-mindedness and a promise of strength to keep them.
settings.readers: The Roman church, to whom Hermas was to pass on the commandments (25:5-7), many of them penitents.

settings.what: The vision of the young shepherd and his sheep
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, on a plain in the country
settings.when: after the charge about the commandments
settings.why: To show what luxury and deceit do to believers, and to tell apart those beyond repentance from those who can still return.
settings.readers: Roman Christians drawn by the pleasures of a rich city, whom the angel of luxury "wears out."

title: Similitude 6.2: The angel of luxury and the angel of punishment
sum: The young shepherd is the angel of luxury and deceit, who leads God's slaves astray with evil desires, some "to death" and some "to ruin" (62:1-2). The skipping sheep are those torn from God for good, who added to their sins and blasphemed: for them there is no repentance. The sheep grazing in one place gave themselves to luxury but did not blaspheme: they have hope of renewal (62:3-4). Then Hermas sees a big, wild-looking shepherd in a white goatskin, with a bag, a knotted staff and a whip, who drives those sheep into thorns and thistles and gives them no rest (62:5-7).

views.H: Seven lines of 62:3-4 are missing in the Athos manuscript and survive in pseudo-Athanasius and the versions (see the variants at 62:3 and 62:4). Without them the two kinds of sheep, and the line between death and ruin, would be lost.
views.N: The distinction of death and ruin is like 1 John 5:16-17 ("There is sin headed toward death"); the blasphemy that has no forgiveness, Mark 3:28-29; the thorns and thistles, Genesis 3:18 and Hebrews 6:8.
views.J: Hermas has already said, "Two angels are with each human being," one of righteousness and one of wickedness (36:1 (Mandate 6.2.1)); the angel of luxury is of the second kind. Daniel too sets angels over peoples (Daniel 10:13, 20-21).
views.D: Whether some sins cannot be forgiven, and whether the church may refuse reconciliation, are asked on the site's cards at Hebrews 6 and 1 John 5. Hermas draws the line at blasphemy and final apostasy, not at sins of the flesh.

settings.what: The vision of the shepherd of punishment
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, on the plain
settings.when: after the young shepherd is explained
settings.why: To show that the troubles of life can be God's punishment and training, which lead the straying back to repentance.
settings.readers: Roman Christians suffering losses, poverty, illness and insults (63:4), who are told that these may be God's discipline rather than his rejection.

title: Similitude 6.3: Punishment that trains
sum: Hermas grieves for the whipped sheep. The big shepherd, the Shepherd explains, is the angel of punishment, one of the righteous angels, put in charge of punishing those who wander from God (63:1-3). His punishments belong to everyday life: losses, need, sickness, unrest, insults (63:4). Those punished often blame the Lord instead of their deeds (63:5). When they have been afflicted enough they are handed over to the Shepherd "for good training," made strong in faith, and serve the Lord with a pure heart; if they repent, they see their deeds, call God a righteous judge, prosper, and suffer no more (63:6).

views.H: Part of 63:6 is missing in A and is printed from the Latin and pseudo-Athanasius (see the variant). Lake's margin cites Psalms 7, 51 and 62 and Matthew 21:22 for 63:6.
views.N: Discipline as a sign of God's love (Hebrews 12:5-11); punishment in this life for the sake of salvation (1 Corinthians 5:5; 11:30-32).
views.J: Confessing God's justice in one's own suffering is the prayer of Daniel 9:14 and Nehemiah 9:33; suffering as a father's discipline is Proverbs 3:11-12.
views.D: Lake sees in the book "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance." Here suffering in this life is paideia, a father's training that leads to repentance and to praise of God's justice (63:6). How the churches read penance and forgiveness after baptism is taken up at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6).

echoes: Hebrews 12:5-11; Proverbs 3:11-12; 1 Corinthians 11:30-32; Psalm 7:11; Psalm 62:12; Daniel 9:14

title: Similitude 6.4: An hour of torment
sum: Hermas asks whether those who live in luxury are tormented as long as they lived in it. "The same time," says the Shepherd, and Hermas protests that this is too little (64:1-2). The Shepherd calls him foolish: an hour of luxury is short, but an hour of torment has the power of thirty days, and a day of torment counts for a year (64:3-4).

views.H: Lake's Greek of Hermas's protest in 64:2 is rebuilt from the Latin (see the variant).
views.N: Paul's "light, momentary trouble" (2 Corinthians 4:17) runs the other way: there, suffering is short and glory long. Hermas's arithmetic is about how long pain is felt and remembered.
views.D: The Shepherd calls these torments those of "everyday life" (63:4), and the chapter measures them in hours, days and years of this life. Hermas speaks separately of death and of "destruction forever" (62:4).

settings.what: Hermas's questions about the time of torment
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas
settings.when: after the explanation of the angel of punishment
settings.why: To show that luxury is short and its cost long, because pleasure is forgotten and pain remembered.
settings.readers: Roman Christians who might think a little indulgence costs little.

title: Similitude 6.5: What counts as luxury
sum: Hermas still does not understand, and the Shepherd explains again. Luxury is forgotten the next day because it is clothed in foolishness; torment, even of one day, is remembered as if for a year, and it makes the sufferer remember the luxury that caused it (65:1-4). What kinds of luxury are harmful? Every act a person does with pleasure: the bad-tempered man's anger, the adulterer, drunkard, slanderer, liar, greedy man and cheat all "live in luxury" in what they do (65:5-6). But there is also a luxury that saves: the pleasure of those who do good (65:7).

views.N: The New Testament vice lists (1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:19-21) and the "cheerful giver" of 2 Corinthians 9:7.
views.D: Hermas's definition makes luxury (tryphē) a matter of the heart's delight in sin, not only of wealth. His approval of pleasure in doing good shows that he does not condemn joy as such.
views.R: Roman moralists, pagan and Christian, preached against luxuria. Hermas widens the word to every sin enjoyed.

title: Similitude 7: Affliction for Hermas's household
sum: A few days later Hermas asks the Shepherd to send the punishing shepherd away from his house, for he is afflicting Hermas badly. He must be afflicted, the Shepherd answers, by order of the glorious angel. Hermas's own sins are many but not enough for this; his household has done great wrongs, and the household cannot be afflicted unless its head is (66:1-3). Hermas says they have repented with their whole heart. The Shepherd answers that the sins of the repentant are not forgiven at once: the penitent must torment his own soul, be humble, and bear suffering, and then God will have compassion and heal (66:4-5). He promises to stay with Hermas and to ask the punishing angel to be gentler (66:6-7).

views.H: At 66:4 the word "at once" is missing in the Athos manuscript and supplied from the versions (see the variant). Without it, the Shepherd's "Not at all" would deny forgiveness, against the rest of the chapter.
views.N: Godly sorrow that brings repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10-11); Joel 2:12-13 (rend your hearts); compare 1 John 1:9 and Luke 18:13-14, where forgiveness follows confession.
views.D: Lake sees in Hermas "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance," and this chapter shows why: after repentance comes a time of affliction and humbling before healing. How churches read forgiveness after baptism is taken up at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6).
views.R: The Roman household was one unit under its head (66:3), so a father's losses fell on wife, children and slaves alike.

settings.what: The Shepherd explains Hermas's afflictions
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, who asks for relief for his household
settings.when: a few days after the vision of the shepherds, on the same plain
settings.why: To explain why the innocent head of a sinful household suffers, and that repentance must be followed by humbling before healing.
settings.readers: Hermas's own household, whose sins and repentance run through the book (3:1-4:3; 7:1); and Roman Christian families who suffered losses together.

title: Similitude 8.1: The great willow and the sticks
sum: Similitude 8 (67-77, 77 verses) is the longest of the first eight Similitudes. Hermas sees a great willow covering plains and mountains, and under its shade all who are called by the Lord's name. A tall glorious angel cuts branches with a sickle and gives each person a small stick, yet the tree stays whole (67:1-4). Then the angel asks for the sticks back and sorts the people by the state of their sticks: dry and moth-eaten, dry, half dry, cracked, part green and part dry, green, green with shoots, and green with shoots and fruit. Most of the crowd hand them back green as they received them (67:5-18).

views.H: Berlin papyrus 6789 holds 67:1-12 (Lake's introduction) and gives some readings Lake follows (67:4, 67:7, 67:11). Two verses (67:10, 67:17) are missing in A; 67:17 is Lake's retranslation from the Latin and Ethiopic.
views.N: Aaron's budding staff (Numbers 17:8, the same word rhabdos in the Greek); the mustard tree that shelters (Matthew 13:31-32); the judgment that begins with God's house (1 Peter 4:17).
views.J: The tree that shelters the nations (Daniel 4; Ezekiel 17; 31) and the testing of the tribes' staffs (Numbers 17) are Jewish images Hermas reworks; Michael as the angel over the people (69:3) is from Daniel 10-12.
views.D: The parable describes a whole church being examined, with most found faithful and many given time to repent. It is one of the book's main texts for a church that can readmit sinners.

settings.what: The vision of the willow and the sticks
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance, with the glorious angel of the Lord
settings.to: Hermas, on the plain
settings.when: after Similitude 7
settings.why: To picture the examination of the whole church by God's law, and the time for repentance given to those whose sticks were not green.
settings.readers: The Roman church of Hermas's time, which had seen persecution, apostasy, quarrels and the drift of rich members into pagan society, all named in 72-76.

title: Similitude 8.2: Crowns, seals and the planting
sum: The angel crowns those whose sticks had shoots and fruit and sends them into the tower, gives seals to those with shoots but no fruit, and to those with green sticks gives white clothing and seals (68:1-4). He leaves the rest to the Shepherd to send "into the walls" as each deserves, warning him to look carefully: anyone who slips past will be tested "at the altar" (68:5). Then the Shepherd plants all the sticks and waters them heavily, for the willow "loves life," and the one who created it wants all to live (68:6-9).

views.N: White robes and palms (Revelation 7:9-14); the crown of life (Revelation 2:10; James 1:12); God's will that all be saved (1 Timothy 2:4, in Lake's margin).
views.D: "Seals" (68:2, 68:4) are, in Hermas, the seal of baptism (93:4). The crowned martyrs and the sealed faithful enter the tower at once; the rest are given time.
views.R: Crowns for victors were the reward of the games; the athlete-martyr is crowned (69:6).

title: Similitude 8.3: The tree is God's law; the angel is Michael
sum: Hermas asks what the tree is. It is God's law given to the whole world, and "this law is the Son of God, preached to the ends of the earth"; the people under it are those who heard and believed (69:2). The great and glorious angel is Michael, who has authority over this people, puts the law into believers' hearts, and checks whether they kept it (69:3). The sticks are the law (69:4). Those who broke it are left to the Shepherd for repentance (69:5). The crowned are those who wrestled with the devil and suffered for the law; those with shoots were afflicted but did not die or deny; those with green sticks walked with a pure heart (69:6-8).

views.H: 69:6 is missing in A and retranslated by Lake from the versions. Lake's English note: in Similitude 9 the glorious angel "is the Son of God"; this, with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit, "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas"; he points to W. Lueken's Michael (Göttingen, 1898) for the question.
views.N: The law written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10); the law given through angels (Galatians 3:19; Acts 7:53); the good news preached to all nations (Matthew 24:14); the wrestling against evil powers (Ephesians 6:12).
views.J: Michael is Israel's "great prince" in Daniel 12:1; in 1 Enoch 20:5 he is "set over the best of humankind, in charge of the people." Hermas gives this Jewish office to the angel over the church.
views.D: Lake, on 69:6-7: "the law means the Christian rule of life, not (as in the N.T.) the Jewish Law." The text does not say whether Michael here is the Son or an angel under the Son (see the section below).
views.R: "Steers" (diakybernōn) is a pilot's word, the helmsman of a ship.

echoes: Jeremiah 31:33; Hebrews 8:10; Galatians 3:19; Daniel 12:1; Daniel 10:13; Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:7; Matthew 24:14; Ephesians 6:12; 1 Enoch 20:5

settings.what: The willow and the sticks explained
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, by the willow on the plain (67:1; 70:2); through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (77:1)
settings.when: after the planting of the sticks
settings.why: To name the tree, the angel and the first groups: the law that is the Son, Michael who watches over its keeping, and the martyrs, confessors and faithful.
settings.readers: A Roman church that remembered its martyrs and confessors (the crowned and the afflicted of 69:6-7), and that heard Michael named, as in Daniel and 1 Enoch, as the angel over God's people.

deep.h: Michael and the Son of God
deep.b: In Similitude 8 the glorious angel who gives the law and judges the sticks is Michael (69:3). In Similitude 9 a "glorious man," with six glorious angels at his right and left, is the Son of God (89:8 (Similitude 9.12.8)), and in Similitude 5 the Son "put the angels over" the people (59:2). The text allows two pictures. In one, Michael and the Son are distinct: the Son is the tree and the law (69:2), and Michael is the angel who sees to the law's keeping, as Michael guards God's people in Daniel and 1 Enoch. In the other, the Son himself appears as the chief angel. Harnack writes that it is "not certain" whether Hermas identifies the Spirit-Son with the chief archangel, and Lake judges that the passages together make Hermas's Christology "very hard to reconstruct."

title: Similitude 8.4: The sticks are returned
sum: After a few days the Shepherd sits in the angel's place and has Hermas tie on a towel and serve him. The people come back group by group and pull up their planted sticks (70:1-3). The first groups are examined: the dry and cut stay dry; of the dry but uncut, some are now green; of the half-dry and cracked, many are green and some even bear fruit, while others are worse (70:4-6).

views.H: Part of 70:1 is missing in A; at 70:2 Lake corrects A's "all the groups" to "in their groups" from 68:8 (see the variant); and he calls the end of 70:6 "obscure and probably corrupt."
views.N: Girding with a towel to serve (John 13:4; Luke 12:37; 17:8).
views.R: A slave tied a towel at his waist to wait at table; Hermas takes that role before the angel.

settings.what: The second examination of the sticks
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: The people of the willow, called by Hermas; Hermas serves the Shepherd
settings.when: a few days after the planting
settings.why: To show how many have changed for the better during the time given for repentance.
settings.readers: Roman Christians who had sinned and were told that time had been given them, and that many had already returned.

title: Similitude 8.5: Many have changed
sum: The examination continues group by group. The green but cracked sticks all come back green and whole, and the Shepherd is glad. The half-and-half sticks return in every state. Even of those with only a little green, most now come back green with shoots and fruit, and the Shepherd is overjoyed (71:1-6).

views.H: All of 71:4 is Lake's retranslation from the Latin and Ethiopic (see the variant).
views.D: The chapter is the hope of the parable: change is possible for every group except the worst, and even the worst-looking sticks can bear fruit.

title: Similitude 8.6: God gives repentance; the first groups explained
sum: "This tree loves life," the Shepherd says: many repented and were saved, so great is the Lord's compassion (72:1). Why not all? God gave repentance to those whose hearts he saw would become pure, and withheld it from those who would repent in hypocrisy (72:2). Hermas asks for the meaning of each group, so that those who broke the seal of their baptism may repent and receive a seal again (72:3). The dry, moth-eaten sticks are apostates and betrayers of the church, who blasphemed and were ashamed of the Lord's name: none of them repented (72:4). The dry but sound sticks are hypocrites with strange teachings, who would not let sinners repent; many of them have repented and live in the walls or even the tower (72:5-6).

views.H: Lake's margin at 72:4 prints James 2:7 (the name pronounced over you). The verb of "broke it" is the perfect of thlaō, "crush."
views.N: Repentance as God's gift (Acts 5:31; 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25); the name called over believers (James 2:7); strange teachings (Hebrews 13:9); apostasy without return (Hebrews 6:4-6; 10:26-29).
views.D: The "strange teachings" that refused repentance to sinners match the rigorism Lake describes in Hermas's circle; Hermas's answer is the possibility of one repentance. Whether believers can fall away for good is asked on the card at Hebrews 6.
views.R: Betrayers (prodotai) of the church point to a time when Christians in Rome could be denounced to the authorities.

echoes: Acts 5:31; Acts 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25; James 2:7; Hebrews 6:4-6; Hebrews 13:9; Matthew 24:10

settings.what: The groups of sticks explained
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, by the willow on the plain (67:1; 70:2); through him the Roman church, which he is to tell (77:1)
settings.when: after all the sticks have been examined
settings.why: To name each kind of believer, from apostates to the faithful, and to tell each one whether repentance is still open and where they will live.
settings.readers: The Roman church in its mixed state: apostates and betrayers, false teachers, the double-minded, the quarrelsome, people tangled in business, rich members living like their pagan neighbors, and many who were good. Hermas is told to read the book there (8:3).

title: Similitude 8.7: The double-minded and the quarrelsome
sum: The half-dry sticks are the double-minded, "neither alive nor dead" (73:1). The half-dry and cracked are double-minded slanderers, always split into factions; repentance is still open to them, and those who repent quickly go into the tower, the slower into the walls (73:2-3). The green but cracked sticks are good, faithful people who were jealous of one another over first places; they repented quickly, but whoever goes back to factions will be thrown out of the tower (73:4-5). The commandments say nothing about first places, only about patience and humility (73:6).

views.H: At 73:1 A adds "in the same way" (κατὰ τὸ αὐτό), which Lake calls "meaningless" and probably a gloss.
views.N: Double-mindedness (James 1:8); factions and slander (Galatians 5:20; Romans 16:17); rivalry for rank among the disciples (Mark 9:33-35; 10:35-45) and Diotrephes (3 John 1:9); peace among yourselves (1 Thessalonians 5:13, Lake's margin).
views.D: "First places" (prōteia) may point to rivalry for leadership in the Roman church, which the Visions warn about its leaders (17:7 (Vision 3.9.7)).
views.R: Honor and precedence ruled Roman social life; Hermas sets against them "patience and ... a person's humility" (73:6).

echoes: James 1:8; Galatians 5:20; Mark 9:33-35; 3 John 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:13; Philippians 2:3; Revelation 3:15-16

title: Similitude 8.8: Business and denial
sum: The half-green sticks are those tangled up in business who do not hold on to the saints: half of them lives and half is dead. Many repented and live in the tower; some fell away for good and denied the Lord because of their business; many were double-minded and can still repent if they do it quickly (74:1-3). The sticks two-thirds green are those who denied in various ways: many repented, many fell away, and some double-minded ones can still repent quickly (74:4-5).

views.N: Entangled in business (2 Timothy 2:4); choked by worries and wealth (Luke 8:14); denial (Matthew 10:33; 26:69-75).
views.D: The chapter shows a graded view of sin and repentance: denial is grave, but many who denied are counted among the repentant. 1 Clement 40-65 notes elsewhere on the site refer to this chapter.
views.R: Commerce tied Romans to pagan associations, oaths and patrons; Hermas sees business as the main road away from the church.

title: Similitude 8.9: The rich who lived with the nations
sum: The sticks two-thirds dry are believers who grew rich and respected among the nations, put on pride, left the truth, did not hold on to the righteous and lived with the pagans, though they kept the faith without its works. Many repented and live in the tower (75:1-2). Others lived with the nations for good and were counted with them (75:3). Others were double-minded or made splits; for them repentance is still open, if it is quick (75:4).

views.N: Faith without works (James 2:14-17); friendship with the world (James 4:4); the rich in the present age (1 Timothy 6:17).
views.D: "They stayed in the faith, but did not do the works of faith" (75:1) puts Hermas close to James. Whether faith without works saves is asked on the site's cards at Romans 3 and James 2.
views.R: Wealth brought honor "among the nations," and honor brought invitations to pagan feasts, offices and alliances. Hermas describes Christians who rose in Roman society and drifted from the church.

title: Similitude 8.10: The good with small faults, and believers without works
sum: The green sticks with dry, cracked tips are good, faithful people who sinned a little through small desires and grudges; most repented quickly and live in the tower; some made worse splits, but they will hardly be lost, because they were always good (76:1-2). The dry sticks with a little green are those who only believed but did lawless works, yet never left God, bore the name gladly and welcomed God's slaves into their homes: they repented without hesitating, and all of them will live in the tower (76:3-4).

views.H: At 76:4 Lake suspects a gap: the Latin and Ethiopic versions each read differently, and Funk suggests "not afraid to suffer" (see the variant).
views.N: Hospitality to God's people (Matthew 25:35; Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 1:5-8); faith without works (James 2:24).
views.D: Hospitality counts heavily in Hermas's judgment (76:3), as in Matthew 25.
views.R: Christians traveling between churches depended on hospitality in members' homes; welcoming them was a public sign of faith.

title: Similitude 8.11: Go and tell everyone to repent
sum: When he has explained all the sticks, the Shepherd sends Hermas: tell everyone to repent and live to God, for the Lord in compassion sent the Shepherd to give repentance to all, though some are not worthy; the Lord is patient and wants the calling made through his Son to be saved (77:1). Hermas hopes all will repent. Those who repent with their whole heart, clean themselves and add no more sins will be healed of their former sins, if they are not double-minded; those who add to their sins condemn themselves to death (77:2-4). "I will show you the rest in a few days" (77:5).

views.H: Much of 77:3-4 is missing in A and retranslated by Lake from the Latin and Ethiopic (see the variants).
views.N: God's patience and will that all repent (2 Peter 3:9, Lake's margin; 1 Timothy 2:4); the calling (Ephesians 4:1; 2 Timothy 1:9).
views.D: The ending sums up the book's teaching of one repentance, offered now to all, with healing for former sins on condition of a changed life; the churches' readings of it are discussed at 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6) and in book.json.
views.R: The commission to "go and tell everyone" makes Hermas a messenger to the Roman church, as in the Visions (8:3).

settings.what: The Shepherd's commission to Hermas
settings.by: The Shepherd, the angel of repentance
settings.to: Hermas, sent to "everyone"
settings.when: after all the sticks are explained
settings.why: To send Hermas to proclaim repentance to all and to state its conditions: whole-hearted repentance, no new sins, no double-mindedness.
settings.readers: Every member of the Roman church, to whom Hermas was to read the book with the elders who led it (8:3).
